Choosing a similarity measure

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/similarity-measures.Rmd
similarity-measures.Rmd

A raw co-occurrence count mixes two things: how strongly two items are associated, and how frequent each of them is. An item that appears in most transactions co-occurs with nearly everything, so the heaviest edges of a count network tend to join the most frequent items whatever their association. Similarity measures separate the two by comparing the observed count with the frequencies of the items involved. van Eck and Waltman (2009) distinguish set-theoretic measures, which relate the count to the sizes of the two item sets (Jaccard, cosine, inclusion, Dice), from probabilistic measures, which relate it to the count expected if the items occurred independently (association strength). They argue that only the probabilistic measure removes the effect of item frequency, and recommend it for normalizing co-occurrence data.

The measures differ in which pairs they bring to the top, and the choice changes the substantive reading of a network. This guide compares the eight measures offered by cooccurrence() on one data set, works through one pair by hand, treats the directed relative measure separately, and closes with rescaling and guidance on choosing.

library(cooccure)

Data

movies holds 1,000 films with an IMDb rating of at least 7.0, released between 1970 and 2024. In the analyses below:

  • Transaction: a film (one row, identified by tconst).
  • Items: its genres, listed in the comma-delimited genres column.
  • Grouping variables (not used here): decade and averageRating.
head(movies, 3)
#>       tconst        primaryTitle startYear                    genres decade averageRating
#> 1  tt0118117     The War at Home      1996                     Drama  1990s           7.0
#> 2 tt10534996               Josep      2020 Animation,Biography,Drama  2020s           7.4
#> 3  tt4686844 The Death of Stalin      2017      Comedy,Drama,History  2010s           7.3
#>   numVotes
#> 1     2733
#> 2     2340
#> 3   126237

How are the measures defined?

Write CijC_{ij} for the number of films that carry both genre ii and genre jj, and fif_i for the number of films that carry genre ii. The measures are:

similarity Weight of the edge between ii and jj
"none" CijC_{ij}
"jaccard" Cij/(fi+fj−Cij)C_{ij} / (f_i + f_j - C_{ij})
"cosine" Cij/fifjC_{ij} / \sqrt{f_i f_j}
"inclusion" Cij/min⁡(fi,fj)C_{ij} / \min(f_i, f_j)
"association" Cij/(fifj)C_{ij} / (f_i f_j)
"dice" 2Cij/(fi+fj)2 C_{ij} / (f_i + f_j)
"equivalence" Cij2/(fifj)C_{ij}^2 / (f_i f_j)
"relative" Cij/∑kCikC_{ij} / \sum_k C_{ik}

The first seven are symmetric and give an undirected network. "relative" divides each row by its own sum, so the weight from ii to jj differs from the weight from jj to ii and the network is directed.

The frequencies fif_i are the frequency column of the node table, which as.data.frame() returns with what = "nodes".

genre_counts <- cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",")
genre_nodes <- as.data.frame(genre_counts, what = "nodes")
subset(genre_nodes, node %in% c("Adventure", "Animation", "Drama"))
#>        node degree strength count_strength frequency
#> 1     Drama     20      812            812       634
#> 5 Adventure     15      195            195       101
#> 6 Animation     15      149            149        75

Drama is on 634 of the 1,000 films, Adventure on 101 and Animation on 75. Adventure and Animation share 39 films. That one pair is followed through the measures below: its Jaccard weight is 39/(101+75−39)=39/137=0.28539 / (101 + 75 - 39) = 39 / 137 = 0.285, its cosine weight 39/101×75=0.44839 / \sqrt{101 \times 75} = 0.448, its Dice weight 78/176=0.44378 / 176 = 0.443, and its equivalence weight 0.4482=0.2010.448^2 = 0.201.

Which pairs rank highest under each measure?

The raw counts rank pairs by volume. With top_n = 3 only the three heaviest edges are kept.

co(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",", similarity = "none", top_n = 3)
#> # cooccurrence: 22 nodes, 3 edges | density: 0.0130 | mean degree: 0.2727 | 1000 transactions
#> # similarity: none | counting: full
#> # possible edges: 231 | isolates: 18
#> # top nodes: Drama(deg=3,str=381), Comedy(deg=1,str=159), Romance(deg=1,str=131), Crime(deg=1,str=91)
#>    from      to weight count
#>  Comedy   Drama    159   159
#>   Drama Romance    131   131
#>   Crime   Drama     91    91

All three edges involve Drama, the most frequent genre: Comedy–Drama (159 films), Drama–Romance (131) and Crime–Drama (91). The ranking says more about how common Drama is than about which genres belong together.

Jaccard divides the count by the number of films carrying either genre.

co(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",", similarity = "jaccard", top_n = 3)
#> # cooccurrence: 22 nodes, 3 edges | density: 0.0130 | mean degree: 0.2727 | 1000 transactions
#> # similarity: jaccard | counting: full
#> # possible edges: 231 | isolates: 16
#> # top nodes: Adventure(deg=1,str=0.2847), Animation(deg=1,str=0.2847), Action(deg=1,str=0.2369), Crime(deg=1,str=0.2369), Comedy(deg=1,str=0.2112)
#>       from        to weight count
#>  Adventure Animation  0.285    39
#>     Action     Crime  0.237    59
#>     Comedy     Drama  0.211   159

Adventure–Animation moves to the top with 0.285, the value computed by hand above, followed by Action–Crime (0.237). Comedy–Drama keeps third place (0.211) despite having the largest count, because both genres are common and appear apart as often as together.

Cosine divides by the geometric mean of the two frequencies, which penalizes a pair of unequal frequencies less than Jaccard does.

co(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",", similarity = "cosine", top_n = 3)
#> # cooccurrence: 22 nodes, 3 edges | density: 0.0130 | mean degree: 0.2727 | 1000 transactions
#> # similarity: cosine | counting: full
#> # possible edges: 231 | isolates: 16
#> # top nodes: Adventure(deg=1,str=0.4481), Animation(deg=1,str=0.4481), Drama(deg=1,str=0.4113), Romance(deg=1,str=0.4113), Action(deg=1,str=0.3831)
#>       from        to weight count
#>  Adventure Animation  0.448    39
#>      Drama   Romance  0.411   131
#>     Action     Crime  0.383    59

Adventure–Animation leads again (0.448), and Drama–Romance (0.411) replaces Comedy–Drama in the top three, reflecting cosine’s more lenient treatment of a frequent genre paired with a less frequent one.

Inclusion (the Simpson coefficient) divides by the frequency of the rarer genre, so it measures how far the rarer genre is contained in the more common one.

co(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",", similarity = "inclusion", top_n = 3)
#> # cooccurrence: 22 nodes, 3 edges | density: 0.0130 | mean degree: 0.2727 | 1000 transactions
#> # similarity: inclusion | counting: full
#> # possible edges: 231 | isolates: 17
#> # top nodes: News(deg=2,str=2), Documentary(deg=1,str=1), Drama(deg=1,str=1), History(deg=1,str=1), Western(deg=1,str=1)
#>         from      to weight count
#>  Documentary    News      1     1
#>      History    News      1     1
#>        Drama Western      1     1

Documentary–News, History–News and Drama–Western all score 1 with a count of 1. News and Western each appear on a single film, so any genre sharing that film includes them completely. Inclusion rewards rare items and needs a min_occur filter before a score of 1 can be read as a subset relation.

Association strength divides by the product of the frequencies, which is proportional to the count expected under independence.

co(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",", similarity = "association", top_n = 3)
#> # cooccurrence: 22 nodes, 3 edges | density: 0.0130 | mean degree: 0.2727 | 1000 transactions
#> # similarity: association | counting: full
#> # possible edges: 231 | isolates: 17
#> # top nodes: News(deg=2,str=0.02271), History(deg=1,str=0.01613), Horror(deg=1,str=0.01136), Sci-Fi(deg=1,str=0.01136), Documentary(deg=1,str=0.006579)
#>         from     to  weight count
#>      History   News 0.01613     1
#>       Horror Sci-Fi 0.01136     2
#>  Documentary   News 0.00658     1

History–News, Horror–Sci-Fi and Documentary–News top the list, each resting on one or two films. The measure compares observed with expected co-occurrence, and for rare genres the expected count is so small that one shared film is far above it. The next section returns to this.

Dice divides twice the count by the sum of the two frequencies.

co(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",", similarity = "dice", top_n = 3)
#> # cooccurrence: 22 nodes, 3 edges | density: 0.0130 | mean degree: 0.2727 | 1000 transactions
#> # similarity: dice | counting: full
#> # possible edges: 231 | isolates: 16
#> # top nodes: Adventure(deg=1,str=0.4432), Animation(deg=1,str=0.4432), Action(deg=1,str=0.3831), Crime(deg=1,str=0.3831), Comedy(deg=1,str=0.3487)
#>       from        to weight count
#>  Adventure Animation  0.443    39
#>     Action     Crime  0.383    59
#>     Comedy     Drama  0.349   159

The ranking matches Jaccard (Adventure–Animation, Action–Crime, Comedy–Drama), with higher weights (0.443 for the first pair). Dice is a monotone function of Jaccard, D=2J/(1+J)D = 2J / (1 + J), so the two measures always rank pairs in the same order.

Equivalence is the square of cosine.

co(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",", similarity = "equivalence", top_n = 3)
#> # cooccurrence: 22 nodes, 3 edges | density: 0.0130 | mean degree: 0.2727 | 1000 transactions
#> # similarity: equivalence | counting: full
#> # possible edges: 231 | isolates: 16
#> # top nodes: Adventure(deg=1,str=0.2008), Animation(deg=1,str=0.2008), Drama(deg=1,str=0.1692), Romance(deg=1,str=0.1692), Action(deg=1,str=0.1468)
#>       from        to weight count
#>  Adventure Animation  0.201    39
#>      Drama   Romance  0.169   131
#>     Action     Crime  0.147    59

The order is the cosine order, and only the spread changes. The top pair is 1.17 times the third under cosine (0.448 against 0.383) and 1.37 times under equivalence (0.201 against 0.147), so equivalence lets weak pairs fade from a weighted drawing.

How do rare items distort the probabilistic measure?

Association strength and inclusion both reach their highest values for pairs of rare items. Dropping genres that appear on fewer than 20 films with min_occur removes pairs resting on one or two films.

co(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",", similarity = "association",
   min_occur = 20, top_n = 5)
#> # cooccurrence: 17 nodes, 5 edges | density: 0.0368 | mean degree: 0.5882 | 998 transactions
#> # similarity: association | counting: full
#> # possible edges: 136 | isolates: 8
#> # top nodes: Animation(deg=2,str=0.008678), Adventure(deg=1,str=0.005149), History(deg=1,str=0.004536), War(deg=1,str=0.004536), Mystery(deg=1,str=0.003811)
#>         from        to  weight count
#>    Adventure Animation 0.00515    39
#>      History       War 0.00454     9
#>      Mystery  Thriller 0.00381    15
#>  Documentary     Music 0.00354    28
#>    Animation   Fantasy 0.00353     9

Five genres fall below 20 films and two films carried only those genres, so the network has 17 genres and 998 films. The top pairs are now Adventure–Animation (0.00515, or 39/(101×75)39 / (101 \times 75)), History–War, Mystery–Thriller, Documentary–Music and Animation–Fantasy. None involves Drama: once frequency is discounted, the strongest associations are between genres that rarely appear apart. Association weights are small numbers because they are ratios to a product of frequencies; their order, not their size, is what they convey.

What does the directed relative measure show?

similarity = "relative" divides each row of the count matrix by its sum. The weight from genre ii to genre jj is the share of all of ii’s co-occurrences that are with jj, so the rows sum to 1 and the two directions of a pair differ. The edge list therefore has one row per direction. To keep the example small, genres on fewer than 100 films are dropped.

genre_shares <- cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                             similarity = "relative", min_occur = 100)
print(genre_shares, n = 8)
#> # cooccurrence: 8 nodes, 52 directed edges | density: 0.9286 | mean degree: 13.0000 | 983 transactions
#> # similarity: relative | counting: full
#> # possible edges: 56 | isolates: 0
#> # top nodes: Drama(deg=14,str=3.693), Comedy(deg=14,str=2.29), Biography(deg=14,str=1.978), Crime(deg=14,str=1.75), Adventure(deg=14,str=1.482)
#>         from          to weight count
#>  Documentary   Biography  0.688    44
#>      Romance       Drama  0.627   131
#>       Comedy       Drama  0.485   159
#>        Crime       Drama  0.440    91
#>    Biography       Drama  0.424    59
#>    Adventure      Action  0.349    44
#>       Action       Drama  0.338    71
#>    Biography Documentary  0.317    44
#> # ... 44 more edges

The header reports 8 genres and 52 directed edges out of 56 possible ordered pairs. The heaviest edge runs from Documentary to Biography (0.688): about two thirds of Documentary’s co-occurrences in this set are with Biography. The reverse edge, Biography to Documentary, weighs 0.317, because Biography is also often paired with Drama. Both directions carry the same count, 44 films.

The row sums behind these shares are the count strengths of the unnormalized network on the same genres.

as.data.frame(cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                           min_occur = 100),
              what = "nodes")
#>          node degree strength count_strength frequency
#> 1       Drama      7      553            553       634
#> 2      Comedy      7      328            328       278
#> 3       Crime      7      207            207       153
#> 4   Biography      7      139            139       108
#> 5   Adventure      7      126            126       101
#> 6      Action      6      210            210       155
#> 7     Romance      6      209            209       160
#> 8 Documentary      5       64             64       152

Documentary has a count strength of 64 and Biography 139, so the two weights are 44/64=0.68844 / 64 = 0.688 and 44/139=0.31744 / 139 = 0.317.

Because the network is directed, the converters keep the direction.

igraph::is_directed(as_igraph(genre_shares))
#> [1] TRUE

as_igraph() returns a directed graph; Exporting networks shows the other formats.

When should weights be rescaled?

Scaling is applied after the similarity measure and changes the spread of the weights, not which pairs are linked. scale = "minmax" maps the weights to the range 0 to 1.

co(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",", similarity = "jaccard",
   scale = "minmax", top_n = 5)
#> # cooccurrence: 22 nodes, 5 edges | density: 0.0216 | mean degree: 0.4545 | 1000 transactions
#> # similarity: jaccard | counting: full | scale: minmax
#> # possible edges: 231 | isolates: 14
#> # top nodes: Adventure(deg=2,str=1.728), Action(deg=2,str=1.559), Animation(deg=1,str=1), Crime(deg=1,str=0.8314), Comedy(deg=1,str=0.7403)
#>       from          to weight count
#>  Adventure   Animation  1.000    39
#>     Action       Crime  0.831    59
#>     Comedy       Drama  0.740   159
#>     Action   Adventure  0.728    44
#>  Biography Documentary  0.714    44

Adventure–Animation, the strongest Jaccard pair, scores 1 and the other weights are fractions of it: Action–Crime is at 0.831 of the top pair. The order is the Jaccard order.

scale = "zscore" expresses each weight in standard deviations from the mean weight, so weights below the mean are negative. A threshold of 1 keeps the edges at least one standard deviation above the mean.

co(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",", similarity = "jaccard",
   scale = "zscore", threshold = 1)
#> # cooccurrence: 22 nodes, 15 edges | density: 0.0649 | mean degree: 1.3636 | 1000 transactions
#> # similarity: jaccard | counting: full | scale: zscore
#> # possible edges: 231 | isolates: 8
#> # top nodes: Action(deg=4,str=9.225), Crime(deg=3,str=7.393), Drama(deg=3,str=7.343), Thriller(deg=3,str=4.957), Adventure(deg=2,str=7.303)
#>         from          to weight count
#>    Adventure   Animation   4.35    39
#>       Action       Crime   3.48    59
#>       Comedy       Drama   3.02   159
#>       Action   Adventure   2.95    44
#>    Biography Documentary   2.88    44
#>        Drama     Romance   2.77   131
#>        Crime    Thriller   2.35    37
#>       Comedy     Romance   2.23    63
#>  Documentary       Music   2.07    28
#>    Biography     History   2.02    23
#> # ... 5 more edges

Fifteen genre pairs are at least one standard deviation above the mean Jaccard weight, the strongest being Adventure–Animation at 4.35. A negative threshold keeps edges above a point below the mean; the default threshold = 0 keeps every edge. The other scalings ("log", "log10", "sqrt", "binary", "proportion") are described in ?cooccurrence.

Which measure to use?

  • Describing the data: "none" shows the counts as they are, and its heaviest edges show where most co-occurrence lies.
  • Bibliometric and scientometric maps: "association", as recommended by van Eck and Waltman (2009), because it removes the effect of item frequency. Pair it with min_occur so that pairs of rare items do not dominate.
  • Overlap of two items’ transactions: "jaccard" or "dice", which rank pairs identically; Jaccard gives lower weights.
  • Pairs of unequal frequency: "cosine" penalizes a frequent item paired with a rare one less than Jaccard does; "equivalence" keeps the cosine order and widens the gaps.
  • Containment: "inclusion" shows when a rare item appears mostly with a common one, again with min_occur.
  • Composition of each item’s ties: "relative" gives, for each item, the share of its co-occurrences going to each other item, as a directed network.

Counting choices are covered in Counting methods, and group comparisons in Comparing groups.

Reference

van Eck, N. J., & Waltman, L. (2009). How to normalize cooccurrence data? An analysis of some well-known similarity measures. Journal of the American Society for Information Science and Technology, 60(8), 1635–1651. https://doi.org/10.1002/asi.21075
